title: Death to Smoochy
full_review:
All is not what it seems inside the candy-colored world of children's television when a popular star in a sequined rainbow suit is replaced by an upstanding rhinoceros in the mean-spirited farce "Death To Smoochy" (Warner Bros.).

Rainbow Randolf (Robin Williams) is every child's favorite TV star. Until of course the whiskey-swigging Randolf is caught taking a bribe from anxious parents eager to have their precious boy get a front seat in his studio audience. Attempting to do some damage control in this disgraceful scandal, conniving network president Frank Stokes (Jon Stewart) puts his senior programming executive, Nora (Catherine Keener), on the job. "Squeaky clean" is the operative word in finding Randolf's immediate replacement. Enter Sheldon Mopes (Edward Norton) and his alter-ego Smoochy, a puffy, fuscia rhino, eerily similar to the popular (and some would say annoying) Barney character.

Concerned for the environment, with unrelenting ethics and not just a little naive, the righteous rhino is an instant hit with the kids. Soon Smoochy's picture is splashed on a huge Times Square billboard (replacing Randolf's), Sheldon is living in the swanky corporate penthouse (Randolf is broke and homeless) and Nora (Randolf's ex-girlfriend) is beginning to take a shining to the hot pink fur ball.

Director Danny DeVito's dark comedy sets up the causes for Randolf's revenge in rather obvious ways. But Williams is a game player, running with the ball. Norton is a fine foil for Williams vengeful antics, without turning his character's "aw-shucks" disposition into a caricature -- though sometimes he comes perilously close. Williams is allowed to do what he does best: rant and rave like a lunatic, except this time with a hard, spiteful edge. It works only sporadically, but becomes off-putting when Randolf's mental stability goes down the tubes. And the distinctive idiosyncracies of both characters grow tiresome all too soon.

Going behind the scenes of a supposedly benign industry to discover it's actually corrupt and filled with back stabbers is not exactly a fresh premise. But the film throws in a few curve balls to spice things up. The mobsters are Irish, not Italian. Punch-drunk boxers and dwarves as well as children fill out Smoochy's cast. The dialogue is smart, and sometimes irreverent, which makes for a few hilarious moments. And the parody bits (Smoochy does an Ice Capade show) work well.

However, the script is a bit derivative. DeVito takes a page from Mel Brooks' book when Randolf sets Smoochy up to perform for a Neo-Nazi group who end up chanting "Heil Smoochy." The ensemble comedy eventually collapses under its own weight, sinking into warped, vicious humor with some gritty violence. And apparently, some even more gruesome scenes were left on the cutting room floor.

Oddly enough, the film is peppered with throw-away lines that make reference to Catholicism. Nora speaks of her first Holy Communion. At a low, desperate moment, Randolf confesses that as a child he wanted to be a priest. Sheldon asks in a tense situation, "What would Jesus do?" These and a few others don't really add up to much, whether as jabs aimed at Catholicism or as positive statements meant to buoy faith. However, Randolf's desire to be a priest may be an indirect attempt to connect homosexuality to the priesthood as Randolf's rabid homophobia poorly veils his sexual orientation.

DeVito, who also stars as Sheldon's smarmy agent in the film, has a leaning toward black humor. His previous efforts, such as "Throw Momma From the Train," "War of the Roses" and "Drowning Mona," had the same type of mean thread running through them. However, after the shock humor and nasty shenanigans are repeated for the nth time in "Death To Smoochy," the audience may understandably tune out.

Due to some spiteful violence, an implied sexual encounter and a variety of sexual references, much rough language and profanity, the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops classification is A-IV -- adults, with reservations. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted. (A-IV) (R) 2002
